content: In 2012, approximately 260,000 children under the age of 15 acquired HIV, with up to 42% of these cases attributed to mother-to-child transmission through breastfeeding. Antiretroviral prophylaxis, administered either to the mother or the infant, has the potential to significantly reduce this mode of transmission. The objective of this review was to identify which antiretroviral prophylactic regimens are both effective and safe in reducing the risk of HIV transmission through breastfeeding, thereby decreasing child morbidity and mortality. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using Cochrane Collaboration methods and relevant databases, including Cochrane CENTRAL, EMBASE, PubMed, LILACS, and Web of Science. The search covered studies published between January 1, 1994, and January 14, 2014. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving HIV-infected mothers who breastfed their infants were included if either the mothers or the infants received antiretroviral prophylaxis for at least four weeks during breastfeeding. A total of 15,922 references were identified, and 81 studies were examined in detail. Seven RCTs met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed. 1. Trial 1: This trial compared triple antiretroviral prophylaxis during pregnancy and breastfeeding with a shorter antiretroviral regimen given to the mother. At 12 months, the triple regimen was associated with lower risks of HIV transmission and combined HIV transmission or death, but there was no difference in infant mortality alone. The quality of evidence for these outcomes was rated as low to moderate. 2. Trial 2: This trial compared two regimens: six months of breastfeeding with zidovudine, lamivudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir versus zidovudine, lamivudine, and abacavir starting from 26–34 weeks of gestation. At six months, there was no significant difference in the risk of infant HIV infection, infant death, or combined HIV infection or death between the two groups. The quality of evidence was very low to low. 3. Trial 3: This trial compared single-dose nevirapine with six weeks of infant zidovudine. At 12 weeks, the risk of HIV infection was higher in the zidovudine group compared to the single-dose nevirapine group. The quality of evidence was very low. 4. Trial 4: A multi-country trial compared single-dose nevirapine with six weeks of infant nevirapine. At 12 months, infants in the extended nevirapine group had a lower risk of mortality compared to the control group. However, there was no difference in the risk of HIV transmission or combined HIV transmission and death. The quality of evidence was low to moderate. 5. Trial 5: This trial evaluated three regimens: single-dose nevirapine plus one week of zidovudine, the control regimen plus nevirapine for up to 14 weeks, and the control regimen with dual prophylaxis for up to 14 weeks. At 24 months, the extended nevirapine group had a lower risk of HIV transmission and combined HIV transmission or death compared to the control group, but no difference in infant mortality alone. Similarly, the dual prophylaxis group had a lower risk of HIV transmission and combined HIV transmission or death compared to the control group, but no difference in infant mortality. There was no significant difference in outcomes between the two intervention arms. The quality of evidence was moderate to high. 6. Trial 6: This trial compared six weeks of nevirapine with six months of nevirapine in infants of mothers not receiving highly active antiretroviral therapy. There was no difference in the risk of HIV infection between the six-month and six-week nevirapine groups. The quality of evidence was low to moderate. 7. Trial 7: This trial compared three groups: maternal triple-drug antiretroviral prophylaxis, infant nevirapine, and no intervention. Infants in the maternal prophylaxis group had a lower risk of HIV infection and combined HIV infection or death compared to the control group, but no difference in infant mortality alone. Similarly, infants receiving extended nevirapine prophylaxis had a lower risk of HIV infection and combined HIV infection or death compared to the control group, but no difference in infant mortality. There was no significant difference in outcomes between the maternal and extended infant prophylaxis groups. The quality of evidence was low to moderate. In conclusion, antiretroviral prophylaxis, whether administered to the HIV-infected mother or the HIV-exposed infant during breastfeeding, is effective in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV. However, further research is needed to address concerns about maternal resistance and the response to subsequent antiretroviral therapy following maternal prophylaxis. An ongoing trial (IMPAACT 1077BF) is currently investigating the efficacy and safety of maternal triple antiretroviral prophylaxis compared to daily infant nevirapine for preventing HIV transmission through breastfeeding.
